title: Documentary & Reportage
subtitle: Report from the ground, narrate a film, and investigate over months

lessons.title: Le reportage
lessons.description: Write and speak like a reporter on the ground: capture atmosphere, restitute testimony, and make a reader feel the scene.

blocks.heading: Le reportage : montrer plutôt que résumer
blocks.body: Reportage differs from a news brief in one essential way: it does not summarise an event, it puts the reader inside it. A reporter who was actually there writes from sensory detail — the mud, the cold, a particular voice — rather than from abstraction. The reader should finish the piece feeling they had been on the terrain themselves, not merely informed that something happened there.

examples.french: Un bon reportage ne résume pas un événement, il y plonge le lecteur.
examples.english: A good piece of reportage does not summarise an event, it plunges the reader into it.

examples.french: Elle s'est rendue sur place plutôt que de se contenter des dépêches.
examples.english: She went to the scene herself rather than settling for the wire reports.

examples.french: Ce qui distingue le reportage, c'est le détail que seul un témoin oculaire peut restituer.
examples.english: What sets reportage apart is the detail only an eyewitness can convey.

examples.french: Le grand reporter écrit avec ses cinq sens, pas seulement avec ses notes.
examples.english: The field correspondent writes with all five senses, not just with their notes.

blocks.tip: If a sentence in your reportage could have been written from a press release without leaving the office, cut it — reportage earns its place by detail that only presence on the ground can supply.

blocks.heading: L'immersion et le carnet de terrain
blocks.body: Immersive reporting begins long before the writing: it begins with the decision to stay, to watch, to let a scene unfold at its own pace instead of asking for a summary. A carnet de terrain filled with small, unglamorous observations — what someone was wearing, the exact words used, the silence after a question — becomes the raw material a polished piece is built from later.

examples.french: Elle s'est immergée trois semaines dans ce quartier avant d'écrire une seule ligne.
examples.english: She immersed herself in this neighbourhood for three weeks before writing a single line.

examples.french: Son carnet de terrain était couvert de détails que personne ne lui avait demandés.
examples.english: Her field notebook was covered in details nobody had asked her for.

examples.french: Prendre des notes sur le vif, c'est accepter de perdre parfois le fil pour gagner en vérité.
examples.english: Taking notes on the fly means sometimes accepting you lose the thread in order to gain in truthfulness.

examples.french: L'immersion suppose de rester bien après que les autres journalistes sont repartis.
examples.english: Immersion means staying well after the other journalists have already left.

blocks.tip: The most quotable line of a reportage is rarely the one a source says on record for the camera — it is the one they say afterward, once they think the notebook is closed.

blocks.heading: Restituer une atmosphère sans la trahir
blocks.body: Restituting an atmosphere is a balancing act: enough sensory detail to make a scene palpable, but never invented detail dressed up as observation. A reporter can describe the ambient noise of a market at dawn only if they actually stood there at dawn; borrowing atmosphere from imagination, however plausible, is where reportage quietly becomes fiction.

examples.french: L'ambiance du camp était palpable dès les premières minutes.
examples.english: The camp's atmosphere was palpable within the first few minutes.

examples.french: Le bruit ambiant du marché couvrait presque entièrement nos voix.
examples.english: The market's ambient noise almost entirely drowned out our voices.

examples.french: Décrire un décor sans jamais l'avoir vu, c'est trahir le pacte du reportage.
examples.english: Describing a setting one has never seen betrays reportage's basic contract with the reader.

examples.french: Chaque détail sensoriel doit pouvoir être attribué à un moment réellement vécu.
examples.english: Every sensory detail must be traceable to a moment that was actually lived through.

blocks.tip: Keep two separate columns in your notes: what you directly observed, and what a source told you they observed — conflating the two is the single most common ethical failure in immersive reportage.

blocks.heading: Le présent de narration pour l'immédiateté du reportage
blocks.body: Even when a piece was written well after the events it describes, reportage often switches into the present tense at the key scene — the présent de narration — to close the distance between reader and moment. A paragraph can move from passé composé, setting up what happened, into the present, dropping the reader directly into the scene as if it were unfolding now.

examples.french: Il est sept heures du matin. La rue est encore vide, mais déjà on entend les premiers camions.
examples.english: It is seven in the morning. The street is still empty, but the first trucks can already be heard.

examples.french: Nous sommes arrivés la veille ; ce matin-là, le village se réveille sous la pluie.
examples.english: We had arrived the day before; that morning, the village wakes up under the rain.

examples.french: Elle avance lentement dans la boue, son carnet serré contre elle.
examples.english: She advances slowly through the mud, her notebook clutched against her.

examples.french: Personne ne parle. On entend seulement le vent et, au loin, un moteur qui tourne.
examples.english: No one speaks. Only the wind can be heard, and, in the distance, an engine running.

blocks.tip: Signal the shift into the présent de narration clearly with a time marker ('ce matin-là', 'à cet instant') — an unmarked, abrupt tense switch reads as a mistake rather than a deliberate stylistic choice.

blocks.heading: Le gérondif et le participe présent pour l'action simultanée
blocks.body: Reportage often needs to show two things happening at once — a reporter moving while observing, a source speaking while a scene continues around them. The gérondif ('en marchant', 'en parlant') attaches a simultaneous action to the sentence's main subject, while the participe présent, used more freely, can describe a cause or a parallel circumstance without a subordinate clause slowing the sentence down.

examples.french: En marchant dans la boue, elle décrivait déjà la scène à voix basse pour son enregistreur.
examples.english: Walking through the mud, she was already describing the scene under her breath for her recorder.

examples.french: Le village, vivant surtout de la pêche, subissait de plein fouet la fermeture du port.
examples.english: The village, living mainly off fishing, was bearing the full brunt of the port's closure.

examples.french: Elle a recueilli ce témoignage en partageant, pendant trois jours, le quotidien de cette famille.
examples.english: She gathered this testimony by sharing this family's daily life for three days.

examples.french: Sachant qu'elle n'aurait qu'une seule chance, elle a posé la question la plus directe possible.
examples.english: Knowing she would only get one chance, she asked the most direct question possible.

blocks.tip: The gérondif requires the same subject for both actions ('en marchant, elle décrivait' — she walks and she describes); if the subjects differ, a full subordinate clause is needed instead.

passages.title: Trois semaines à Valcourbe
passages.french:
Léa Nadaud n'avait prévu de rester à Valcourbe que trois jours. Elle y resta trois semaines.
Le village vivait autrefois de sa conserverie de poisson, fermée depuis six mois. Léa aurait pu écrire ce reportage depuis Paris, à partir des chiffres du chômage. Elle choisit de le vivre de l'intérieur.
Elle logea chez Odile, une ancienne ouvrière, dans une chambre qui sentait le sel et le bois humide. Chaque matin, elle descendait au port avec son carnet de terrain, notant tout : l'heure exacte où les bateaux ne sortaient plus, le silence inhabituel sur les quais, la façon dont les hommes évitaient de se regarder.
« Personne ne viendra filmer ça longtemps, lui dit un jour un pêcheur. Vous, vous êtes encore là après trois semaines. »
Ce fut cette phrase, glissée en passant, qui devint la première ligne de son reportage.
Elle refusa d'écrire une seule scène qu'elle n'avait pas vue de ses propres yeux. Un habitant lui raconta une rixe survenue la veille de son arrivée ; elle nota le récit, mais le publia comme un témoignage rapporté, jamais comme une scène vécue.
Le bruit ambiant du port vide, les mouettes tournant sans but au-dessus des bateaux à quai, l'odeur de sel sans poisson : chaque détail sensoriel venait d'un moment réellement observé.
Son reportage parut un dimanche. Il ne contenait aucun chiffre du chômage. Il commençait par une phrase, et se terminait par un silence — celui du port, à l'aube, un matin d'octobre.
passages.english:
Léa Nadaud had only planned to stay in Valcourbe for three days. She stayed three weeks.
The village used to live off its fish cannery, closed for six months. Léa could have written this piece from Paris, using unemployment figures. She chose to live it from the inside.
She lodged with Odile, a former factory worker, in a room that smelled of salt and damp wood. Every morning, she went down to the harbour with her field notebook, noting everything: the exact hour the boats stopped going out, the unusual silence on the docks, the way the men avoided looking at each other.
"No one will come and film this for long," a fisherman told her one day. "You're still here after three weeks."
It was this sentence, dropped in passing, that became the first line of her piece.
She refused to write a single scene she had not seen with her own eyes. A resident told her about a brawl that had happened the day before her arrival; she noted the account, but published it as reported testimony, never as a scene she had witnessed.
The empty harbour's ambient noise, the seagulls circling aimlessly above the moored boats, the smell of salt without fish: every sensory detail came from a moment actually observed.
Her piece appeared on a Sunday. It contained not a single unemployment figure. It began with a sentence, and ended with a silence — the harbour's, at dawn, one October morning.

lessons.title: Le documentaire
lessons.description: Write and read documentary commentary: the narration that guides a viewer through images without ever competing with them.

blocks.heading: Le commentaire au service de l'image
blocks.body: Documentary commentary — the voix off — has one job the image cannot do alone: supply context, chronology, or meaning the picture does not carry by itself. Good commentary never describes what the viewer can already see; it says only what the image, on its own, cannot tell them. The moment narration starts describing the obvious, the viewer stops trusting it.

examples.french: Le commentaire ne décrit jamais ce que l'image montre déjà.
examples.english: The commentary never describes what the image already shows.

examples.french: La voix off apporte ce que le plan, à lui seul, ne peut pas dire.
examples.english: The voice-over supplies what the shot, on its own, cannot say.

examples.french: Un bon narrateur se tait dès que l'image parle pour elle-même.
examples.english: A good narrator falls silent as soon as the image speaks for itself.

examples.french: Le texte et l'image doivent se compléter, jamais se répéter.
examples.english: Text and image must complement each other, never repeat each other.

blocks.tip: Watch a rough cut with the sound off first — if you cannot tell what a scene needs explained, you are not yet ready to write its commentary.

blocks.heading: Construire un documentaire : scène, archive, entretien
blocks.body: A documentary is assembled, not simply filmed: scenes shot in the present alternate with archival footage and with intervenants speaking directly to camera. The montage decides how these three materials talk to each other — a striking image of archive footage placed right after a claim in an interview can support it, undercut it, or complicate it, all without a single word of commentary.

examples.french: Le montage alterne images du présent et archives soigneusement choisies.
examples.english: The edit alternates present-day footage and carefully chosen archival images.

examples.french: Chaque intervenant apporte un point de vue que le montage vient ensuite nuancer.
examples.english: Each contributor brings a viewpoint that the edit then goes on to nuance.

examples.french: Une reconstitution doit toujours être signalée comme telle, jamais confondue avec des images réelles.
examples.english: A reenactment must always be flagged as such, never mistaken for real footage.

examples.french: Le réalisateur a mis six mois à trouver le bon ordre entre archive et présent.
examples.english: The director spent six months finding the right order between archive and present-day footage.

blocks.tip: Reenactments (reconstitutions) sit in a grey zone documentaries must handle carefully — a viewer who cannot tell reenacted footage from real footage has been misled, however unintentionally.

blocks.heading: Le rythme : plans, silences, respiration
blocks.body: Documentary pacing works like prose: not every second needs commentary, and a well-placed silence can carry more weight than an explanation. Editors alternate gros plans, which slow the viewer down onto a single detail, with plans larges, which restore context and breathing room — a documentary shot entirely in close-up exhausts an audience just as surely as a text with no paragraph breaks.

examples.french: Un gros plan ralentit le regard ; un plan large lui redonne de l'air.
examples.english: A close-up slows the eye down; a wide shot gives it room to breathe again.

examples.french: Le silence qui suit cette phrase en dit plus qu'un commentaire n'aurait pu.
examples.english: The silence following that line says more than any commentary could have.

examples.french: Le rythme du documentaire épouse celui de la parole, jamais l'inverse.
examples.english: The documentary's rhythm follows that of the speech, never the other way around.

examples.french: Trop de gros plans d'affilée finit par fatiguer le spectateur.
examples.english: Too many close-ups in a row eventually tires the viewer out.

blocks.tip: If you cannot justify a cut's timing beyond 'it felt right', watch the sequence again against the interviewee's own breathing — pacing that fights natural speech rhythm rarely survives an audience's patience.

blocks.heading: L'impersonnel et le passif pour la neutralité du commentaire
blocks.body: Documentary commentary favours constructions that keep the camera's eye, not a personal voice, in the foreground: "on y voit", "on découvre", and the passive "il est filmé" describe what appears on screen without inserting the narrator's own presence. This impersonal register lets the commentary stay neutral even when the images themselves are dramatic.

examples.french: On y voit un village entier suspendu à la même question.
examples.english: In it, we see an entire village hanging on the same question.

examples.french: Ce document n'avait jamais été montré au public jusqu'ici.
examples.english: This document had never been shown to the public until now.

examples.french: On découvre, au fil des images, une histoire que personne n'avait racontée.
examples.english: As the images unfold, a story no one had ever told comes into view.

examples.french: Cette scène a été filmée sans que les intervenants le sachent.
examples.english: This scene was filmed without the contributors knowing it.

blocks.tip: Avoid 'je' in commentary almost entirely — even a first-person documentary usually restricts it to the moments where the filmmaker's own presence is itself part of the story.

blocks.heading: Le présent de vérité générale et l'imparfait de contexte
blocks.body: Commentary moves between two tenses with distinct roles: the present for statements that remain true regardless of when the film is watched ("la ville compte aujourd'hui..."), and the imparfait to set the historical context the images require ("à l'époque, personne n'imaginait..."). Mixing them without care blurs whether a fact still holds or belongs only to the past being shown.

examples.french: La ville compte aujourd'hui deux fois moins d'habitants qu'en 1990.
examples.english: Today the city has half as many inhabitants as in 1990.

examples.french: À l'époque, personne n'imaginait que l'usine fermerait un jour.
examples.english: At the time, no one imagined the factory would ever close.

examples.french: Ce que ces images montrent reste, encore aujourd'hui, largement méconnu.
examples.english: What these images show remains, even today, largely unknown.

examples.french: Le quartier vivait alors au rythme des trois usines qui l'entouraient.
examples.english: The neighbourhood back then lived by the rhythm of the three factories surrounding it.

blocks.tip: If a commentary line could be read on any future viewing and stay true, use the present; if it only describes the moment captured on screen, the imparfait keeps that distinction honest.

passages.title: Le montage de « La dernière usine »
passages.french:
Yanis Belhadj avait tourné plus de deux cents heures de rushes pour son documentaire sur la fermeture de l'usine textile de Rouvray. Il en garda un peu moins de deux.
« On ne raconte pas une histoire en gardant tout, lui rappela sa monteuse, Camille. On la raconte en choisissant ce qu'on enlève. »
Le premier montage durait trois heures et racontait tout, dans l'ordre exact du tournage. Camille le trouva épuisant. « Trop de gros plans d'affilée, dit-elle. Le spectateur n'a jamais le temps de respirer. »
Elle proposa d'alterner : une archive en noir et blanc de l'usine dans les années soixante, puis un plan large de l'usine aujourd'hui, silencieuse, avant de revenir à un intervenant.
Yanis hésita sur le commentaire. Sa première version décrivait chaque image en détail. « Le commentaire ne décrit jamais ce que l'image montre déjà, lui rappela Camille. Dis-nous plutôt ce qu'on ne voit pas. »
Il réécrivit une phrase : au lieu de « On voit ici l'usine fermée », il écrivit « À l'époque, personne n'imaginait que l'usine fermerait un jour. » La phrase donnait un sens à l'image, sans jamais la doubler.
Une seule scène posa un vrai dilemme : celle du dernier jour de production, qu'aucune caméra n'avait filmée. Camille proposa une reconstitution, brève, clairement signalée à l'écran par un carton : « Scène reconstituée d'après plusieurs témoignages. »
Le film fut diffusé un jeudi soir. Il durait quatre-vingt-dix minutes. Il ne contenait ni voix off omniprésente, ni musique dramatique. Seulement des images, un silence bien placé, et, de temps en temps, une phrase qui disait ce que l'image, seule, ne pouvait pas dire.
passages.english:
Yanis Belhadj had shot over two hundred hours of footage for his documentary about the closure of the Rouvray textile factory. He kept a little under two.
"You don't tell a story by keeping everything," his editor, Camille, reminded him. "You tell it by choosing what to remove."
The first cut ran three hours and told everything, in the exact order it had been filmed. Camille found it exhausting. "Too many close-ups in a row," she said. "The viewer never gets a chance to breathe."
She suggested alternating: black-and-white archive footage of the factory in the sixties, then a wide shot of the factory today, silent, before returning to a contributor.
Yanis hesitated over the commentary. His first draft described every image in detail. "The commentary never describes what the image already shows," Camille reminded him. "Tell us instead what we can't see."
He rewrote one line: instead of "Here we see the closed factory", he wrote "At the time, no one imagined the factory would ever close." The sentence gave the image meaning, without ever doubling it.
Only one scene posed a real dilemma: the last day of production, which no camera had filmed. Camille suggested a brief reenactment, clearly flagged on screen with a caption: "Scene reenacted based on several accounts."
The film aired on a Thursday evening. It ran ninety minutes. It contained no ever-present voice-over, no dramatic music. Only images, a well-placed silence, and, now and then, a sentence saying what the image, alone, could not.

lessons.title: L'enquête au long cours
lessons.description: Build a long-form investigation: cultivate sources, corroborate claims across months of work, and argue a conclusion the reader can trust.

blocks.heading: L'enquête au long cours : le temps comme méthode
blocks.body: A long-form investigation differs from daily news reporting in one defining trait: it treats time itself as part of the method. Months of patient recouping, verifying, and waiting for a second source to confirm a first one are not a delay before the real work — they are the real work. An investigation published too early, before every claim has been corroborated, risks collapsing the very story it set out to prove.

examples.french: L'enquête au long cours ne se mesure pas en jours, mais en mois de recoupements.
examples.english: A long-form investigation is measured not in days, but in months of cross-checking.

examples.french: Publier trop tôt, c'est parfois détruire une enquête qui aurait pu tenir.
examples.english: Publishing too early can sometimes destroy an investigation that could have held up.

examples.french: Chaque allégation a été vérifiée par au moins deux sources indépendantes.
examples.english: Every allegation was verified by at least two independent sources.

examples.french: Des mois d'enquête ont été nécessaires avant la première ligne publiée.
examples.english: Months of investigation were necessary before a single published line.

blocks.tip: Treat every single-source claim as provisional, however credible the source seems — the discipline of waiting for corroboration is what separates investigation from rumour.

blocks.heading: Sources, anonymat et déontologie
blocks.body: A source who agrees to speak sous couvert d'anonymat is trusting a journalist with something that could cost them their job, their safety, or worse — a trust the déontologie of the profession treats as close to sacred. Protecting a source's identity is not a favour granted case by case; it is a professional obligation that holds even under legal pressure to reveal it.

examples.french: Elle a accepté de témoigner sous couvert d'anonymat, par peur de représailles.
examples.english: She agreed to speak on condition of anonymity, for fear of reprisals.

examples.french: Le secret des sources n'est pas négociable, même face à un tribunal.
examples.english: Protection of sources is not negotiable, even in the face of a court.

examples.french: Un lanceur d'alerte risque souvent bien plus que le journaliste qui le cite.
examples.english: A whistleblower often risks far more than the journalist who quotes them.

examples.french: Un informateur fiable ne remplace jamais un document qui le corrobore.
examples.english: A reliable informant never replaces a document that corroborates them.

blocks.tip: A good investigative journalist can usually explain, precisely, why they believe an anonymous source — vague trust ('il m'a semblé honnête') is not deontology, it is a shortcut around it.

blocks.heading: Recouper, corroborer, établir les faits
blocks.body: Between a first tip and a publishable claim lies a whole discipline: recouper means checking one account against another, corroborer means finding independent confirmation, and établir les faits means only stating, in the end, what has survived both. A single dramatic document is a lead, not a conclusion, until it has been checked against everything else the investigation has gathered.

examples.french: Nous avons recoupé ce document avec trois témoignages distincts.
examples.english: We cross-checked this document against three separate accounts.

examples.french: Rien n'a été publié tant que les faits n'étaient pas pleinement établis.
examples.english: Nothing was published until the facts were fully established.

examples.french: Une pièce à conviction ne suffit jamais, seule, à établir un fait.
examples.english: A single piece of evidence is never, alone, enough to establish a fact.

examples.french: Corroborer une allégation prend souvent plus de temps que la découvrir.
examples.english: Corroborating an allegation often takes longer than discovering it in the first place.

blocks.tip: Keep a written trail of exactly how each fact was corroborated — an investigation that cannot show its work, if challenged later, loses credibility even when its conclusions were correct.

blocks.heading: Le plus-que-parfait dans le récit d'enquête
blocks.body: A months-long investigation rarely unfolds in a straight line, and the plus-que-parfait is the tense that keeps its chronology honest: it marks what had already happened before another past event the reader is now following. Without it, a reader cannot tell whether a document was found before or after a source came forward — a distinction that can be the whole substance of the investigation's argument.

examples.french: La source avait déjà contacté deux autres journaux avant de nous appeler.
examples.english: The source had already contacted two other papers before calling us.

examples.french: Quand nous avons obtenu le document, l'enquête interne avait été close depuis un mois.
examples.english: By the time we obtained the document, the internal inquiry had been closed for a month.

examples.french: Elle avait recoupé l'information trois fois avant d'accepter de la publier.
examples.english: She had cross-checked the information three times before agreeing to publish it.

examples.french: Le lanceur d'alerte avait tenté d'alerter sa hiérarchie bien avant de se tourner vers la presse.
examples.english: The whistleblower had tried to alert their superiors well before turning to the press.

blocks.tip: In an investigation, always ask 'what had already happened by this point?' before writing a paragraph — the plus-que-parfait is often what separates a clear timeline from a confusing one.

blocks.heading: Les connecteurs de concession et d'argumentation
blocks.body: A long investigation must weigh contradicting evidence honestly, and French offers precise connectors for exactly that: néanmoins introduces a fact that stands despite what came before, en dépit de attaches a concession directly to a noun, and quoi qu'il en soit closes an argument by setting aside a remaining uncertainty without pretending it does not exist. These connectors let an investigative conclusion sound careful rather than either overconfident or evasive.

examples.french: La source n'avait aucun document ; son témoignage fut néanmoins retenu, après recoupement.
examples.english: The source had no documents; their testimony was nonetheless kept, after cross-checking.

examples.french: En dépit de plusieurs mises en demeure, l'enquête a été publiée intégralement.
examples.english: In spite of several legal warnings, the investigation was published in full.

examples.french: Quoi qu'il en soit, aucune ligne n'a été publiée sans une seconde source.
examples.english: Be that as it may, no line was published without a second source.

examples.french: Certains détails restent, néanmoins, impossibles à corroborer entièrement.
examples.english: Some details remain, nevertheless, impossible to fully corroborate.

blocks.tip: 'Quoi qu'il en soit' is not a way to dismiss doubt — used well, it names the doubt explicitly and then explains why the conclusion holds regardless, which is more convincing than pretending no doubt remains.

passages.title: Neuf mois pour une ligne
passages.french:
Farid Chennoufi reçut le premier document un mardi de janvier, glissé dans une enveloppe sans expéditeur. Il ne le publia qu'en septembre.
Le document, seul, semblait accablant : il suggérait qu'une filiale avait maquillé ses comptes pendant trois ans. Farid savait qu'une pièce à conviction ne suffit jamais, seule, à établir un fait.
Il passa les premières semaines à recouper l'écriture, le papier, la mise en page du document avec des originaux déjà publics. Tout correspondait. Ce n'était qu'un début.
Une première source, ancienne comptable de l'entreprise, accepta de parler sous couvert d'anonymat. Elle confirma certains chiffres, mais pas tous. « Je n'ai vu que ce que mon poste me permettait de voir », précisa-t-elle honnêtement.
Farid chercha alors une deuxième source, puis une troisième. L'une d'elles s'était déjà adressée, en vain, à un régulateur deux ans plus tôt — un détail que Farid ne découvrit qu'en juillet, et qui changea complètement la portée de l'enquête.
En dépit d'une mise en demeure reçue en août, le journal maintint sa décision de publier. « Quoi qu'il en soit, dit la rédactrice en chef, aucune ligne ne sortira sans une seconde source. C'est non négociable. »
La dernière vérification prit trois semaines de plus. Un expert-comptable indépendant confirma, chiffres à l'appui, ce que les trois témoignages laissaient entendre.
L'enquête parut en septembre, sur douze pages. Elle avait nécessité neuf mois de travail, six sources, et une seule pièce à conviction qui, seule, n'avait jamais suffi.
passages.english:
Farid Chennoufi received the first document on a Tuesday in January, slipped into an envelope with no return address. He did not publish it until September.
The document alone seemed damning: it suggested a subsidiary had falsified its accounts for three years. Farid knew that a single piece of evidence is never, alone, enough to establish a fact.
He spent the first weeks cross-checking the handwriting, the paper, the layout of the document against already-public originals. Everything matched. It was only a beginning.
A first source, a former accountant at the company, agreed to speak on condition of anonymity. She confirmed some figures, but not all of them. "I only saw what my position allowed me to see," she noted honestly.
Farid then sought a second source, then a third. One of them had already approached, in vain, a regulator two years earlier — a detail Farid only discovered in July, and one that completely changed the scope of the investigation.
In spite of a legal warning received in August, the paper stood by its decision to publish. "Be that as it may," said the editor-in-chief, "not a single line will go out without a second source. That is not negotiable."
The final check took three more weeks. An independent accountant confirmed, figures in hand, what the three accounts had suggested.
The investigation appeared in September, across twelve pages. It had required nine months of work, six sources, and a single piece of evidence which, alone, had never been enough.
